title: The New Kingdom
subtitle: 1550–1200 BC · Empire, the Amarna Rupture and the Ramesside Recovery

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From Ahmose's expulsion of the Hyksos through the Thutmosid conquests, the Amarna rupture and the Ramesside recovery to Merneptah

entries.label: Ahmose I — the expulsion of the Hyksos
entries.hint: Ahmose I completed the war his father Seqenenre and brother Kamose had fought: he took Avaris, chased the Hyksos into southern Canaan and besieged them at Sharuhen, then turned south to break a Nubian revolt. Egypt was one kingdom again for the first time in a century and a half, and the reign is conventionally the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom. The soldier Ahmose son of Ibana of el-Kab left the fullest eyewitness account.
entries.note: Autobiography of Ahmose son of Ibana, tomb at el-Kab: translation Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.12–15. Tell el-Dab'a (Avaris) end-of-Hyksos horizon: Bietak, Avaris (1996). Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.207–14.

entries.label: Amenhotep I — consolidation and the necropolis founded
entries.hint: Amenhotep I ruled a peaceful, consolidating reign, campaigning only lightly in Nubia and Libya. He and his mother Ahmose-Nefertari were later worshipped for centuries as the patron gods of the Theban west bank and are the traditional founders of the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina. His tomb has never been securely identified, and he may have been the first king to separate tomb from mortuary temple, the pattern the Valley of the Kings then followed.
entries.note: Deir el-Medina cult of Amenhotep I and Ahmose-Nefertari: Jaroslav Černý, A Community of Workmen at Thebes in the Ramesside Period (1973). The Abbott and other Ramesside tomb-robbery papyri place his tomb intact in their day. Shaw (2000) pp.218–20.

entries.label: Thutmose I — to the Euphrates and past the Fourth Cataract
entries.hint: Thutmose I, of non-royal birth, campaigned further in both directions than any Egyptian king before him: south beyond the Fourth Cataract, where a boundary stela at Tombos records the crushing of Kush, and north across Syria to the Euphrates, where he set up a stela on the 'inverted water that runs backwards'. He is also the first king with a securely identified tomb in the Valley of the Kings.
entries.note: Tombos stela (year 2) and the Euphrates campaign: Urkunden IV (Sethe) 82–103; Redford, Egypt, Canaan, and Israel in Ancient Times (1992) pp.148–51. Tomb KV38 (and KV20, shared with Hatshepsut): Reeves & Wilkinson, The Complete Valley of the Kings (1996).

entries.label: Thutmose II — a short reign and a Nubian revolt
entries.hint: Thutmose II, son of Thutmose I by a secondary wife, reigned only a few years. An Aswan inscription records his army suppressing a revolt in Kush with orders to kill every male. He married his fully royal half-sister Hatshepsut; their daughter was Neferure, and the future Thutmose III was his son by a lesser wife, Isis. His mummy shows a man dead in his thirties.
entries.note: Aswan/Sehel inscription of the Kush revolt: Urkunden IV 137–41. Reign length debated (3–13 years); Luc Gabolde, 'La chronologie du règne de Thoutmosis II', SAK 14 (1987). Mummy (Cairo CG 61066), Deir el-Bahari cache.

entries.label: Hatshepsut — the woman who ruled as king
entries.hint: Hatshepsut began as regent for her infant stepson Thutmose III and within about seven years had taken the full kingly titulary and male regalia, ruling roughly two decades of prosperity and building. Her terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari, her pair of Karnak obelisks and the reliefs of her trading expedition to Punt are among the period's masterworks. Late in Thutmose III's reign her name and images were systematically hacked from many monuments — a delayed act, probably about succession legitimacy rather than personal spite.
entries.note: Deir el-Bahari (Djeser-djeseru): excavated by Naville (EEF) and the Metropolitan Museum; Polish–Egyptian restoration since 1961. The proscription's late date: Charles Nims, 'The Date of the Dishonoring of Hatshepsut', ZÄS 93 (1966); Roehrig (ed.), Hatshepsut: From Queen to Pharaoh (2005).

entries.label: Thutmose III — the empire at its greatest extent
entries.hint: Once he ruled alone, Thutmose III led at least seventeen campaigns into the Levant across twenty years, opening with the victory at Megiddo, breaking the Mitanni-backed coalition of Syrian princes, and crossing the Euphrates to raid Mitannian territory. Egypt's empire reached from the Fourth Cataract of the Nile to northern Syria. His campaign annals, carved on the walls at Karnak from the daybook of the army, are the fullest military record of the ancient Near East.
entries.note: Annals of Thutmose III, Karnak: Urkunden IV 645–756; translation in Redford, The Wars in Syria and Palestine of Thutmose III (2003). Empire overview: Shaw (2000) pp.238–48.

entries.label: Amenhotep II — holding the empire by fear
entries.hint: Amenhotep II advertised his own strength — a stela at Giza claims no one could draw his bow — and put down Syrian resistance with calculated brutality: his campaign stelae record bringing home the bodies of seven princes of Takhsy hung head-down from the prow of his ship, six then displayed on the walls of Thebes and one sent to Napata as a warning. After his reign the northern empire settled into a stable frontier with Mitanni.
entries.note: Memphis and Karnak stelae of Amenhotep II: Urkunden IV 1281–1315; translation in Pritchard (ed.), Ancient Near Eastern Texts (ANET, 1969) pp.245–48. Der Manuelian, Studies in the Reign of Amenophis II (1987).

entries.label: Thutmose IV — the Dream Stele and peace with Mitanni
entries.hint: Thutmose IV set a granite stela between the paws of the Great Sphinx recording a dream in which the sun god promised him the throne if he cleared the sand from the monument — a legitimising story for a king who may not have been the designated heir. His reign ended the long cold war with Mitanni by marriage: he took a daughter of King Artatama I as a wife, the first of several such Egyptian–Mitannian royal marriages.
entries.note: Dream Stele, Giza: Urkunden IV 1539–44; Zivie-Coche, Sphinx: History of a Monument (2002). Mitanni marriage: the Amarna letters (EA 29) refer back to it; Betsy Bryan, The Reign of Thutmose IV (1991).

entries.label: Amenhotep III — the reign of magnificence
entries.hint: Amenhotep III ruled nearly forty years of peace and unmatched wealth, fed by Nubian gold and Levantine tribute. He built on a colossal scale — the Luxor temple, the largest-ever mortuary temple behind the Colossi of Memnon, the Malkata palace-city, a temple at Soleb in Nubia — issued series of commemorative scarabs recording his marriages, lion hunts and a pleasure lake dug in fifteen days, and corresponded as an equal with the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and Arzawa. Late in the reign he promoted the sun-disc, the Aten, as a special royal cult.
entries.note: Commemorative scarabs: Blankenberg-van Delden, The Large Commemorative Scarabs of Amenhotep III (1969). Malkata and the mortuary temple: Kozloff & Bryan (eds.), Egypt's Dazzling Sun: Amenhotep III and his World (1992). Amarna letters from his reign: Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992).

entries.label: Akhenaten — the Aten and the abandoned capital
entries.hint: Amenhotep IV changed his name to Akhenaten, declared the sun-disc Aten the sole god, built a new capital, Akhetaten, on virgin ground in Middle Egypt, and eventually closed the temples of Amun and had the god's name chiselled out across Egypt. Court art broke every convention — elongated bodies, intimate family scenes, the king shown with his queen Nefertiti as near-equals. Cuneiform letters from vassals and allies pile up unanswered while the empire's northern grip loosened.
entries.note: Boundary stelae of Akhetaten: Murnane & Van Siclen, The Boundary Stelae of Akhenaten (1993). Amarna letters: William L. Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992). Surveys: Dodson, Amarna Sunrise (2014); Barry Kemp, The City of Akhenaten and Nefertiti: Amarna and its People (2012).

entries.label: Neferneferuaten and Smenkhkare — the contested succession
entries.hint: Akhenaten's last years and immediate aftermath are the murkiest in Egyptian royal history. A co-ruler using the throne name Ankhkheperure appears — under the name Neferneferuaten (with feminine grammar in some writings, so probably Nefertiti or a royal daughter ruling as king) and, separately or successively, as a male Smenkhkare. Within a few years all were gone and the child Tutankhaten held the throne.
entries.note: The 'Coregency Stela' (recut), Amarna letters EA dating, and the KV55 burial. Competing reconstructions: James Allen, 'The Amarna Succession', in Brand & Cooper (eds.), Causing His Name to Live (2009); Aidan Dodson, Amarna Sunset (2009); Marc Gabolde, D'Akhenaton à Toutânkhamon (1998).

entries.label: Tutankhamun — the restoration of the old gods
entries.hint: Tutankhaten came to the throne at about nine, changed his name to Tutankhamun, abandoned Amarna, and issued a Restoration Stela describing the land as neglected and the gods' shrines fallen, and himself as putting it right — the work in practice of the courtiers Ay and Horemheb. He died at eighteen or nineteen with no surviving heir. His near-intact tomb, found by Howard Carter in 1922, made him the most famous of all Egyptian kings despite a minor reign.
entries.note: Restoration Stela (Cairo CG 34183), from Karnak: Urkunden IV 2025–32. Tomb KV62: Carter & Mace, The Tomb of Tut·ankh·Amen (1923–33); Reeves, The Complete Tutankhamun (1990). CT/DNA study of the mummy: Hawass et al., JAMA 303 (2010).

entries.label: Ay — the courtier who buried the king and took the throne
entries.hint: Ay, an elderly 'god's father' who had been a senior figure since Akhenaten's reign and probably Nefertiti's relative, performed the Opening of the Mouth ritual at Tutankhamun's funeral — shown doing so on the tomb wall, in kingly dress — and then reigned about four years himself. A letter from Tutankhamun's widow to the Hittite king asking for a prince to marry, which ended with the prince murdered en route, is usually read against this succession.
entries.note: Ay in KV62's burial-chamber painting; his own tomb WV23. The 'Dahamunzu affair': the Hittite 'Deeds of Suppiluliuma' (Güterbock, JCS 10, 1956); identification of the widow debated (Ankhesenamun most likely). Schneider, 'The Hittite–Egyptian correspondence', in various.

entries.label: Horemheb — the general who reset the state
entries.hint: Horemheb, army commander and 'deputy of the king' under Tutankhamun, took the throne without royal blood and governed as a restorer: a Great Edict (preserved at Karnak) against official corruption and abuse of the poor, the dismantling of the Amarna temples for fill in his own pylons, and the writing of Akhenaten, Neferneferuaten, Tutankhamun and Ay out of the king-lists so that his own reign followed straight on from Amenhotep III. Childless, he named his vizier and general Paramessu as heir.
entries.note: Great Edict of Horemheb, Karnak: Urkunden IV 2140–62; Kruchten, Le Décret d'Horemheb (1981). His Memphite (pre-royal) tomb at Saqqara and royal tomb KV57: Martin, The Memphite Tomb of Horemheb (1989).

entries.label: Ramesses I — the founder from the army
entries.hint: Paramessu, a career soldier and vizier from a military family of the eastern Delta, became Ramesses I on Horemheb's death, already old. He reigned little more than a year — long enough to begin the great hypostyle hall at Karnak and to raise his son Seti to co-regent — and is the founder of the Nineteenth Dynasty, the Ramesside line.
entries.note: Tomb KV16. Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions I; Kitchen, Pharaoh Triumphant: The Life and Times of Ramesses II (1982) pp.15–18. His mummy, taken to North America in the 19th c., was returned to Egypt in 2003.

entries.label: Seti I — the recovery of the empire
entries.hint: Seti I set out to win back what had slipped since Amarna: campaign reliefs on the north wall of the Karnak hypostyle hall show him retaking Canaan, striking the Hittites' Syrian clients, and a clash with the Hittite army near Kadesh. At home he built the finely carved Abydos temple with its king-list, completed much of the Karnak hall, and cut the largest and most elaborately decorated tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV17.
entries.note: Karnak war reliefs: The Epigraphic Survey, The Battle Reliefs of King Sety I (1986). Abydos temple and king-list: Calverley & Broome, The Temple of King Sethos I at Abydos (1933–58). KV17: Reeves & Wilkinson, The Complete Valley of the Kings (1996).

entries.label: Ramesses II — sixty-six years and the Hittite peace
entries.hint: Ramesses II reigned about sixty-six years, the defining Ramesside reign. Year 5 brought the near-disaster and claimed victory at Kadesh against the Hittites; Year 21, a sworn peace treaty with Hatti, later sealed by his marriage to a Hittite princess. He moved the capital to a new city, Pi-Ramesses, in his Delta homeland, and built more than any other king — Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum, additions at Karnak, Luxor, Abydos and Memphis, and colossal statues everywhere, fathering perhaps a hundred children.
entries.note: Kitchen, Pharaoh Triumphant: The Life and Times of Ramesses II (1982); Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II. Pi-Ramesses (Qantir/Tell el-Dab'a): Pusch & Herold, magnetometer survey, Ägypten und Levante (1990s). Tomb KV7; his mummy, Cairo.

entries.label: Merneptah — the Libyan war and the Israel Stele
entries.hint: Merneptah, already elderly as Ramesses II's thirteenth son and long-serving crown prince, faced in his fifth year a large invasion of the western Delta by a Libyan king allied with northern sea-raiders — Ekwesh, Shekelesh, Lukka, Sherden, Teresh. He defeated it in a six-hour battle and recorded the victory at Karnak and on a stela that lists his subdued enemies, including the earliest known written mention of Israel, 'laid waste, its seed is not'.
entries.note: Great Karnak Inscription and the 'Israel Stela' (Cairo JE 31408, reused from Amenhotep III): translation in ANET pp.376–78; Manfred Görg and the 'Israel' debate, e.g. Michael Hasel, Domination and Resistance (1998). Colleen Manassa, The Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah (2003).

entries.label: The disputed end of the Nineteenth Dynasty
entries.hint: After Merneptah the dynasty fractured: his son Seti II held the throne against a rival, Amenmesse, who ruled the south for a few years; then the boy-king Siptah under the powerful chancellor Bay, a foreigner later executed on the king's order; and finally Seti II's widow Tawosret as sole female king. Setnakhte seized power around 1189 and founded the Twentieth Dynasty, remembering the preceding years — in the later Great Harris Papyrus — as a time when 'Egypt was in the hands of chiefs and rulers of towns'.
entries.note: Amenmesse: Rolf Krauss and Frank Yurco's competing reconstructions. Bay's execution: Ostracon IFAO 1864 (Grandet, BIFAO 100, 2000). Tawosret's tomb KV14. Retrospective: Great Harris Papyrus (P. BM EA 9999); Grandet, Le papyrus Harris I (1994). This coda's later phase runs just past this folio's close.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Syrian and Nubian wars of empire, Megiddo and Kadesh, and the first Libyan and Sea Peoples raids

entries.label: Ahmose takes Avaris and Sharuhen
entries.hint: Ahmose I's forces stormed the Hyksos capital Avaris and then pursued the survivors into southwest Canaan, besieging them for three years at Sharuhen before taking it. The soldier Ahmose son of Ibana, rewarded with 'gold of valour' and captives after each action, describes fighting on the water at Avaris and the fall of Sharuhen in his tomb autobiography — the campaign that ended a century of foreign rule in the north.
entries.note: Autobiography of Ahmose son of Ibana, el-Kab; Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.12–15. Avaris destruction horizon: Bietak, Avaris (1996). Sharuhen usually located at Tell el-Ajjul or Tell el-Far'ah (South).

entries.label: The conquest of Kush to the Fourth Cataract
entries.hint: Across the first century of the New Kingdom, Egypt turned Nubia from a raided frontier into an annexed province. Ahmose and Amenhotep I broke the early revolts, Thutmose I pushed the border past the Fourth Cataract with the Tombos stela, and Thutmose III fixed Napata, below Gebel Barkal, as the southern limit. Temple-towns at Soleb, Sesebi and Sai and a settled Egyptian administration replaced the fortresses, and Nubian gold became the empire's financial backbone.
entries.note: Tombos stela: Urkunden IV 82–86. Nubian temple-towns: Morris, The Architecture of Imperialism (2005); Stuart Tyson Smith, Wretched Kush (2003). Napata frontier: Kendall, 'Gebel Barkal', in various.

entries.label: The Battle of Megiddo
entries.hint: In his twenty-third year Thutmose III marched against a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian princes led by the ruler of Kadesh and backed by Mitanni, gathered at Megiddo. Against his officers' advice he took the army single-file through the narrow Aruna pass and emerged unopposed on the plain. The enemy broke at the first clash but the Egyptians stopped to loot, and the city held out through a seven-month siege before surrendering — the earliest battle in history recorded in tactical detail.
entries.note: Annals of Thutmose III, Karnak (the 'Gebel Barkal' and Armant stelae supplement): Urkunden IV 647–67; Redford, The Wars in Syria and Palestine of Thutmose III (2003) pp.7–36. Analysis: Cline, The Battles of Armageddon (2000).

entries.label: Thutmose III breaks Mitanni's coalition
entries.hint: Over sixteen further campaigns Thutmose III dismantled Mitanni's influence in Syria: he took the ports of the Levantine coast to supply his army by sea, stormed the inland strongholds, and in his thirty-third year crossed the Euphrates on boats carried overland from Byblos to raid Mitannian territory and set up a stela beside his grandfather's. He hunted 120 elephants in the marshes of Niya on the way home. The northern empire he left ran to the Orontes and beyond.
entries.note: Annals, Urkunden IV 689–734; the Gebel Barkal Stela (Boston MFA 23.733) on the Euphrates crossing and the elephant hunt. Redford, The Wars in Syria and Palestine of Thutmose III (2003).

entries.label: Amenhotep II's campaigns of terror
entries.hint: Amenhotep II campaigned twice in Syria early in his reign, and his stelae dwell on cruelty as policy: he personally killed seven rebel princes of the district of Takhsy, brought their bodies back hanging head-down from his ship's prow, and had six hung on the enclosure wall of Thebes and the seventh sent upriver to be displayed at Napata 'to make manifest the victories of the king forever'. After this the Syrian frontier stabilised and formal peace with Mitanni followed under his son.
entries.note: Memphis and Karnak stelae of Amenhotep II: Urkunden IV 1288–1309; ANET pp.245–48. Der Manuelian, Studies in the Reign of Amenophis II (1987) pp.62–91.

entries.label: The Battle of Kadesh
entries.hint: In his fifth year Ramesses II marched on Kadesh and was fed false intelligence that the Hittite army under Muwatalli II was far to the north. His four divisions strung out, and Hittite chariots ambushed the second as it made camp, scattering it and nearly overrunning the king. Ramesses rallied with his guard and a relief column arriving from the coast until the Hittites withdrew into the city. Egypt held the field but not the objective; both sides claimed victory, and Ramesses covered temple walls with the story in a 'Poem', a 'Bulletin' and battle reliefs.
entries.note: The Kadesh texts: Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II 2–147; translation Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions Translated II (1996). The Hittite side: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005) pp.234–41. Murnane, The Road to Kadesh (2nd ed. 1990).

entries.label: The Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty
entries.hint: Sixteen years after Kadesh, Ramesses II and Hattusili III swore a treaty of permanent peace, non-aggression, mutual defence against attack and against internal revolt, and the extradition of fugitives, with the gods of both lands as witnesses. It survives as an Egyptian version carved at Karnak and the Ramesseum and as Akkadian cuneiform tablets from the Hittite capital — the only ancient international treaty preserved from both parties, and the model for a plaque at the United Nations.
entries.note: Egyptian version: Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II 225–32. Hittite (Akkadian) tablets from Hattusa: Edel, Der Vertrag zwischen Ramses II. und Hattušili III. (1997). The treaty is dated to Ramesses II's Year 21.

entries.label: Merneptah's Libyan war
entries.hint: In Merneptah's fifth year the Libyan king Merey led his people, with their households and cattle, into the western Delta alongside allied sea-raiders — Ekwesh, Shekelesh, Lukka, Sherden and Teresh, some of the earliest 'Sea Peoples' named. Egyptian forces met and destroyed them at a place called Perire, killing some six thousand and taking thousands of prisoners; Merey fled. It was the first of the great western and northern assaults that would define the end of the Bronze Age.
entries.note: Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah: Manassa, The Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah (2003); the Athribis and Cairo 'Israel' stelae supplement. Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014) pp.1–10, 121–28 on the wider context.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The empire's administration — the viceroy of Kush, the vizierate, the army as a career, and the workmen's village of Deir el-Medina

entries.label: The Viceroy of Kush
entries.hint: Egypt governed conquered Nubia through a single powerful officer, the 'King's Son of Kush' — a crown appointee, not a royal son — with deputies for Wawat (Lower Nubia) and Kush (Upper Nubia), his own treasury, and command of a Nubian levy. He shipped the annual gold quota north, oversaw the temple-towns, and installed the sons of surviving Nubian chiefs, raised Egyptian-style, as local headmen. The office ran for four centuries and made Nubia the most tightly held part of the empire.
entries.note: Reisner, 'The Viceroys of Ethiopia', JEA 6 (1920); George Reisner and later Labib Habachi. Synthesis: Morris, The Architecture of Imperialism (2005) pp.79–115; Stuart Tyson Smith, Wretched Kush (2003).

entries.label: Ruling Canaan by vassalage
entries.hint: In the Levant, Egypt annexed almost no territory. It held a handful of garrison and supply centres — Gaza, Jaffa, Beth Shan, Kumidi — staffed them with 'overseers of northern foreign lands', and left the local city-kings in place, bound by loyalty oath, an annual tribute in kind, the obligation to feed passing Egyptian troops, and the surrender of a son to be schooled at the Egyptian court. The Amarna letters are the day-to-day paperwork of this system fraying.
entries.note: Amarna letters: Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992). The garrison system: Morris, The Architecture of Imperialism (2005); Redford, Egypt, Canaan, and Israel in Ancient Times (1992) pp.192–213.

entries.label: The two viziers and the Duties of the Vizier
entries.hint: By the reign of Thutmose III the vizierate was split into a Southern vizier at Thebes and a Northern vizier at Memphis/Heliopolis, each the chief judge and head of the civil administration for his half of Egypt. The tomb of the Theban vizier Rekhmire carries the fullest texts on the office anywhere — the 'Installation of the Vizier', a royal charge to judge impartially and fear no one, and the 'Duties of the Vizier', a long list of what crossed his desk.
entries.note: Tomb of Rekhmire (TT100): Norman de Garis Davies, The Tomb of Rekh-mi-Rē' at Thebes (1943); Urkunden IV 1071–1108. van den Boorn, The Duties of the Vizier (1988).

entries.label: Deir el-Medina — the royal tomb-makers' village
entries.hint: The men who cut and decorated the royal tombs lived in a walled state village in a desert valley, sealed off from the Nile. The workforce was split into a left and right 'side' under two foremen and a scribe; it was paid monthly in grain, fish, wood, water and other rations delivered from state stores, and settled most of its own disputes in a local court. Its rubbish heaps and the tombs above yielded tens of thousands of inscribed limestone flakes — the most intimate documentation of any ancient working community.
entries.note: Bruyère's excavations for IFAO (1922–51); Jaroslav Černý, A Community of Workmen at Thebes in the Ramesside Period (1973); Lesko (ed.), Pharaoh's Workers (1994); Toivari-Viitala, Women at Deir el-Medina (2001).

entries.label: The Great Edict of Horemheb
entries.hint: Horemheb's reform law, carved on a stela at Karnak, targets the abuse of ordinary people by the state's own agents: soldiers and inspectors who seize boats, hides, grain and labour 'for the pharaoh' and keep them. It prescribes heavy penalties — cutting off the nose, exile to the frontier fort of Sile — sets up regional courts of trusted priests and officials, forbids them to take bribes, and has the king tour the country hearing cases in person.
entries.note: Edict of Horemheb, Karnak: Urkunden IV 2140–62; Kruchten, Le Décret d'Horemheb (1981); translation in Murnane, Texts from the Amarna Period in Egypt (1995) pp.235–40.

entries.label: The army becomes a career
entries.hint: The New Kingdom fielded a permanent army: numbered divisions named for gods (Amun, Ra, Ptah, Seth), an elite chariotry with its own training and stables, archers, and growing contingents of foreign professionals — Sherden marines, Nubian bowmen, Libyan units. Soldiering became a path to land, tax exemption and office; Horemheb and Ramesses I rose from it to the throne. Scribal 'satires' that mock the soldier's lot are the flip side of how attractive the career had become.
entries.note: Alan Schulman, Military Rank, Title and Organization in the Egyptian New Kingdom (1964); Anthony Spalinger, War in Ancient Egypt: The New Kingdom (2005). The 'Satire on the Trades' / Papyrus Lansing and Papyrus Anastasi military passages: Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976).

entries.label: Justice by oracle
entries.hint: Alongside the courts, New Kingdom Egyptians took disputes to a god. At Deir el-Medina the carried image of the deified Amenhotep I was asked yes-or-no questions on feast days — often about property, unpaid debts or the identity of a thief — and answered by 'nodding' toward one of two written statements or dipping as the bearers felt it move. The verdicts were written down and treated as binding, and the same procedure settled boundary and inheritance cases at temples across the country.
entries.note: Černý, 'Egyptian Oracles', in Parker, A Saite Oracle Papyrus (1962); McDowell, Jurisdiction in the Workmen's Community of Deir el-Medîna (1990) pp.107–41. Ramesside oracle ostraca and papyri from the village.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The empire of Amun, the Aten heresy and its reversal, and the democratised journey through the Book of the Dead

entries.label: The empire of Amun
entries.hint: Amun-Ra of Thebes became the god of empire: kings credited him with their victories, gave him a fixed share of war plunder, foreign tribute and captured land, and enlarged his temple at Karnak into the largest religious building complex ever raised. His annual Opet festival carried his image in procession from Karnak to Luxor to renew the king's divinity, and his oracle could name the next king. By Amenhotep III's reign the Amun priesthood and estates were a power in their own right — part of what Akhenaten's revolution was reacting against.
entries.note: Karnak's growth: Blyth, Karnak: Evolution of a Temple (2006). Opet festival: Epigraphic Survey, The Festival Procession of Opet in the Colonnade Hall (1994). Amun's economic weight: on the later Wilbour and Harris papyri, but the trajectory is Eighteenth-Dynasty.

entries.label: Akhenaten's one god
entries.hint: Akhenaten's Aten was the physical sun-disc itself, shown only as a disc whose rays end in hands, worshipped in temples open to the sky rather than dark sanctuaries, and — uniquely in Egyptian religion — treated as the sole god, with the king and his family the only intermediaries. The Great Hymn to the Aten, found in a courtier's tomb at Amarna, praises the disc as sole creator of all lands and peoples. Whether this counts as true monotheism or a royal cult of one god is still argued.
entries.note: Great Hymn to the Aten, tomb of Ay at Amarna: Murnane, Texts from the Amarna Period (1995) pp.112–16; Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.96–100. Assmann, Moses the Egyptian (1997); Hornung, Akhenaten and the Religion of Light (1999).

entries.label: The undoing of Amarna
entries.hint: Within a generation the revolution was cancelled. Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela describes the temples as ruined and the gods as having turned their backs, and restores their endowments; Horemheb and Seti I re-carved Amun's erased name across Egypt and quarried the Aten temples for building fill; and the king-lists jump straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb, deleting four reigns. Later texts refer to Akhenaten only as 'the enemy' or 'the criminal of Akhetaten'.
entries.note: Restoration Stela (Cairo CG 34183): Urkunden IV 2025–32. The dismantled Aten temples (talatat) recovered from Karnak pylon fill: Redford, The Akhenaten Temple Project (1976– ). Later condemnation formulae: Murnane, Texts from the Amarna Period (1995).

entries.label: The Book of the Dead
entries.hint: The New Kingdom repackaged the afterlife literature as the 'Book of Going Forth by Day' — around two hundred spells, written on a papyrus roll laid in the coffin, often illustrated. Spell 125 stages the dead person's denial of a list of sins before Osiris and forty-two assessors while the heart is weighed against the feather of maat; Spell 6 animates the shabti figures that will do the deceased's forced labour in the next world. Copies were produced for stock with a blank left for the buyer's name.
entries.note: Standard reference: Erik Hornung, The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Afterlife (1999); Raymond Faulkner, The Ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead (1985). The Papyrus of Ani (BM EA 10470) is the best-known illustrated copy.

entries.label: The hidden tomb and the books of the night
entries.hint: New Kingdom kings split the royal burial in two: a mortuary temple on the edge of the cultivation for the public offering cult, and a concealed rock-cut tomb in a remote desert valley on the west of Thebes. The tomb walls carry a new genre of guidebooks to the twelve hours of the night — the Amduat, the Book of Gates, the Litany of Ra — mapping the sun god's passage through the underworld and his rebirth at dawn, a journey the dead king merges into.
entries.note: Reeves & Wilkinson, The Complete Valley of the Kings (1996). The underworld books: Erik Hornung, The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Afterlife (1999). Theban West Bank mortuary temples: overview in Wilkinson, The Complete Temples of Ancient Egypt (2000).

entries.label: Abydos and the pilgrimage of every Egyptian
entries.hint: Abydos and its Osiris cult reached their fullest form under the Nineteenth Dynasty. Seti I built a limestone temple of exceptional relief quality with seven sanctuaries and the Abydos king-list, and behind it the 'Osireion', a subterranean cenotaph symbolising Osiris's tomb. Officials of every rank still sought a memorial chapel or stela along the processional way so as to share, after death, in the god's annual festival — the afterlife of Osiris now open, in principle, to anyone.
entries.note: Temple of Seti I: Calverley & Broome, The Temple of King Sethos I at Abydos (1933–58). Osireion: Frankfort, The Cenotaph of Seti I at Abydos (1933). The votive landscape: O'Connor, Abydos (2009) pp.111–35.

entries.label: The gods who hear the poor
entries.hint: Ramesside stelae, especially from Deir el-Medina, show a strikingly personal religion: workmen address Amun as one 'who comes at the voice of the poor man in distress', and men publicly confess a fault — a false oath, contempt for a god — and thank the deity, often the cobra-goddess Meretseger of the Theban peak or Ptah, for the blindness or sickness sent as punishment and then lifted. The deified Amenhotep I, Hathor and household protectors round out a crowded devotional world.
entries.note: Battiscombe Gunn, 'The Religion of the Poor in Ancient Egypt', JEA 3 (1916); Jan Assmann, Egyptian Solar Religion in the New Kingdom (1995); the Deir el-Medina votive stelae, e.g. the stela of Neferabu (BM EA 589).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Temple architecture at imperial scale, the painted Theban tomb, Amarna naturalism and the love poetry

entries.label: The temple at imperial scale
entries.hint: The New Kingdom fixed the classic Egyptian temple: a walled 'mansion of the god' entered through a towered pylon into open courts, a forest of columns in a dark hypostyle hall, then progressively smaller and lower rooms to the sanctuary of the cult image. Karnak grew by accretion as each king added a pylon, court or obelisk; its great hypostyle hall — 134 columns, the central twelve over twenty metres tall — was raised by Seti I and Ramesses II. The scale was a statement of the god's, and the empire's, resources.
entries.note: Blyth, Karnak: Evolution of a Temple (2006); Wilkinson, The Complete Temples of Ancient Egypt (2000). Great Hypostyle Hall: William J. Murnane & the Karnak Hypostyle Hall Project (Brand).

entries.label: The painted Theban tomb-chapel
entries.hint: The officials of the Eighteenth-Dynasty empire cut decorated chapels into the Theban hillside — Nakht, Menna, Sennefer, Rekhmire, Ramose and dozens more. Their painted walls show the banquet with musicians and guests in transparent linen, the estate at harvest, the funeral procession, and files of Nubians, Syrians and Aegeans bringing tribute: a genre of secular painting unmatched elsewhere in the Bronze Age. The tomb of Ramose, half in the old style and half in Amarna style, records the moment the conventions changed.
entries.note: Norman & Nina de Garis Davies, numerous Theban tomb publications for the Egypt Exploration Society and Metropolitan Museum (1910s–40s). Overview: Melinda Hartwig, Tomb Painting and Identity in Ancient Thebes (2004).

entries.label: The Amarna style
entries.hint: Akhenaten's artists broke every rule of the timeless ideal: early on, elongated skulls and jaws, heavy hips, drooping bellies and spidery fingers on the whole royal family; later, a softer naturalism. Sunk relief replaced raised, and formal smiting scenes gave way to the king kissing a daughter or the family eating. A plastered-up room in the house of the sculptor Thutmose held the study heads for these works, among them the painted bust of Nefertiti.
entries.note: Bust of Nefertiti (Ägyptisches Museum, Berlin) and the Thutmose workshop finds: Ludwig Borchardt's Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft excavation, 1912. Style: Cyril Aldred, Akhenaten and Nefertiti (1973); Dorothea Arnold, The Royal Women of Amarna (1996).

entries.label: The love songs
entries.hint: Ramesside papyri and ostraca preserve cycles of secular love poetry in which a young man and woman, calling each other 'brother' and 'sister', long for each other across a garden, a river or a feigned illness. Sensuous, witty and entirely this-worldly, with no gods and no moral, they are the high point of Egyptian lyric and have close formal echoes in the biblical Song of Songs.
entries.note: Chief sources: Papyrus Chester Beatty I, Papyrus Harris 500, the Turin love-song papyrus, and the Cairo love-song ostracon. Editions: Michael V. Fox, The Song of Songs and the Ancient Egyptian Love Songs (1985); Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.181–93.

entries.label: Tales, myths and the new wisdom
entries.hint: New Kingdom prose ranges widely: the folktale-rich Tale of the Two Brothers, the Doomed Prince, and the Taking of Joppa (a Trojan-horse-style ruse); the earthy, satirical Contendings of Horus and Seth; and, in wisdom, the Instruction of Any on family life and the Instruction of Amenemope, a set of thirty chapters on the 'silent' modest man whose sayings run parallel, sometimes almost verbatim, to a section of the biblical Book of Proverbs.
entries.note: Two Brothers (P. d'Orbiney / BM EA 10183); Contendings (P. Chester Beatty I). Amenemope (P. BM EA 10474): Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.146–63, 203–11; the Proverbs 22:17–24:22 parallel, first noted by Adolf Erman (1924).

entries.label: The colossus and the multiplied king
entries.hint: New Kingdom kings put their own image everywhere at maximum size: Amenhotep III's two seated 'Colossi of Memnon', eighteen metres high, fronting a vanished temple; the four twenty-metre rock-cut Ramesses figures at Abu Simbel; the fallen granite colossus of the Ramesseum that inspired Shelley's 'Ozymandias'. Ramesses II also recut hundreds of earlier kings' statues with his own name — statuary as a saturation medium for royal presence.
entries.note: Colossi of Memnon and Amenhotep III's temple: Hourig Sourouzian's conservation project reports. Abu Simbel: Desroches-Noblecourt & Kuentz, Le petit temple d'Abou Simbel (1968). Usurped statuary: Magen, Steinigung und Fluch (on royal name practice); Kitchen, Pharaoh Triumphant (1982).

entries.label: The New Kingdom ensemble
entries.hint: Tomb and temple scenes show music expanding: alongside the old arched harp and flutes come the long-necked lute, the lyre and the double reed-pipe, several of them adopted from the Levant, played in large mixed ensembles at banquets and in temple ritual. Blind male harpers sing the 'Harper's Songs', some of which openly doubt the afterlife and urge enjoyment of the day. Bands of female musicians (the khener) served Amun, and a pair of metal trumpets was buried with Tutankhamun.
entries.note: Lise Manniche, Music and Musicians in Ancient Egypt (1991). Harper's Songs: Lichtheim, 'The Songs of the Harpers', JNES 4 (1945); the 'Song from the Tomb of King Intef' preserved in P. Harris 500. Tutankhamun trumpets: Cairo JE 62007/62008.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Ebers and Edwin Smith medical papyri, the water-clock, star ceilings and the school texts

entries.label: The great medical papyri
entries.hint: The Ebers Papyrus, about twenty metres long, gathers more than seven hundred remedies and diagnostic passages, organised loosely by body part, together with a 'Book of the Heart' that treats the heart as the centre of a system of vessels (metu) carrying blood, air, water and disease. It mixes careful empirical prescription with incantation without seeing a contradiction. The Hearst, Berlin and London medical papyri overlap with it, showing a shared, copied professional literature.
entries.note: Ebers Papyrus (Leipzig University Library), said to be from a Theban tomb, acquired by Georg Ebers 1873. Translation and study: Bendix Ebbell, The Papyrus Ebers (1937); John Nunn, Ancient Egyptian Medicine (1996).

entries.label: Water clocks and star ceilings
entries.hint: To time night rituals the New Kingdom used the outflow water clock — a stone vessel with a small basal hole and interior hour-scales for each month, the oldest example inscribed for Amenhotep III at Karnak. Ceilings in the tomb of Senenmut and later in royal tombs and the Ramesseum carry astronomical diagrams: the decan stars, the northern constellations around a hippopotamus and bull's-leg, and personified planets — the first attempts to picture the whole sky as a system.
entries.note: Karnak clepsydra of Amenhotep III (Cairo CG 37525): Borchardt, Die altägyptische Zeitmessung (1920). Senenmut ceiling (TT353): Dorman, The Monuments of Senenmut (1988). Neugebauer & Parker, Egyptian Astronomical Texts II–III (1964–69).

entries.label: The scribal schools and the miscellanies
entries.hint: Boys destined for administration learned to write by copying — first signs and formulae, then Middle Kingdom classics kept as set texts for a thousand years, then 'miscellanies': anthologies of model letters, hymns and essays that relentlessly praise the scribe's clean, powerful life against the misery of the farmer, soldier and labourer. Thousands of these practice copies survive on limestone flakes and boards, and literacy stayed the preserve of perhaps one person in a hundred.
entries.note: Late Egyptian Miscellanies: Alan Gardiner, Late-Egyptian Miscellanies (1937); Ricardo Caminos, Late-Egyptian Miscellanies (1954). School practice: John Baines & C.J. Eyre, 'Four notes on literacy', GM 61 (1983).

entries.label: Knowledge as lists — the onomastica
entries.hint: Egyptian scholarship expressed itself less in argument than in ordered lists. The Onomasticon of Amenemope, compiled around the end of the New Kingdom, sets out to name 'all things that exist' and runs through the sky and its waters, the earth, ranks of people from king to herdsman, Egyptian towns north to south, then buildings, land types, cereals and cuts of meat — an attempt to hold the whole ordered world in a single classified catalogue.
entries.note: Alan H. Gardiner, Ancient Egyptian Onomastica, 3 vols. (1947). Related: the Ramesseum Onomasticon (Middle Kingdom) and the later Tanis and Hood onomastica.

entries.label: The Dream Book
entries.hint: A Ramesside papyrus from Deir el-Medina lays out a systematic dream manual: page after page of 'If a man sees himself in a dream doing X — good' or 'bad', followed by a short interpretation, sometimes working by opposites or by wordplay on the thing dreamed. It is the earliest known attempt to codify dream interpretation as a reference discipline rather than a one-off priestly reading.
entries.note: Papyrus Chester Beatty III (BM EA 10683), from Deir el-Medina: Alan Gardiner, Hieratic Papyri in the British Museum, Third Series: Chester Beatty Gift (1935). Study: Kasia Szpakowska, Behind Closed Eyes: Dreams and Nightmares in Ancient Egypt (2003).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Nubian and Levantine gold and tribute, the temple estates, and the first recorded strike

entries.label: Nubian gold and the tribute economy
entries.hint: Empire ran on inflows the crown controlled: an annual gold quota carried north from Wawat and Kush, a yearly tribute in kind from the Levantine vassal cities, war plunder, and lavish 'gifts' from the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and Hatti. Tomb and temple walls show the ordered files of foreigners delivering it. Egyptian gold became so abundant that Near Eastern kings begged for it by the hundredweight, and the surplus built temples and endowed cults rather than circulating as money.
entries.note: Tribute (inw) scenes: e.g. tomb of Rekhmire (TT100). The gold-begging letters: Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992), esp. EA 16, 19, 26–27. Analysis: Warburton, State and Economy in Ancient Egypt (1997); Liverani, Prestige and Interest (1990).

entries.label: The rise of the temple estates
entries.hint: Kings endowed the great gods — above all Amun of Thebes — with a growing permanent base of farmland, herds, orchards, ships, workshops, mines and dependent labour, funded by war booty and confirmed by decree. Over the New Kingdom the temples came to control a large fraction of Egypt's arable land and workforce; the later Wilbour land register and the Great Harris Papyrus, which totals Ramesses III's donations, show the scale the trend reached. The institution was stable, tax-favoured, and increasingly a rival to the palace.
entries.note: Wilbour Papyrus (Brooklyn): Alan Gardiner, The Wilbour Papyrus (1941–52). Great Harris Papyrus (P. BM EA 9999): Grandet, Le papyrus Harris I (1994) — Ramesside, but the growth curve is Eighteenth-Dynasty; Barry Kemp, Ancient Egypt: Anatomy of a Civilization (2006) pp.248–60.

entries.label: A grain-and-metal economy without coin
entries.hint: There was no coined money. Wages were paid in grain, and everything else was valued against fixed weights of copper (the deben, about 91 grams, and its tenth) or, for costly goods, silver and gold. Deir el-Medina ostraca record the villagers buying and selling among themselves — a bed, a coffin, a donkey, a slave-woman's labour-days — by stating each item's value in deben and settling in a bundle of commodities that added up. It was a monetised way of thinking without the coin.
entries.note: Jac. J. Janssen, Commodity Prices from the Ramessid Period (1975); Janssen, 'Prolegomena to the Study of Egypt's Economic History', SAK 3 (1975). The village sale and loan ostraca.

entries.label: Copper and turquoise from Sinai and the Arabah
entries.hint: The crown pushed metal extraction beyond the Nile: seasonal expeditions to Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai for turquoise and copper, leaving inscribed stelae and a temple of Hathor 'Lady of Turquoise', and large open-cast and shaft mining with on-site smelting at Timna in the Arabah, where an Egyptian mining shrine to Hathor was built and later reused by local Midianites. The camps show Egyptian overseers directing a mixed local and imported workforce.
entries.note: Sinai: Gardiner, Peet & Černý, The Inscriptions of Sinai (1952–55). Timna: Beno Rothenberg, Timna: Valley of the Biblical Copper Mines (1972); the Hathor shrine (Site 200) and Egyptian New Kingdom pottery. Erez Ben-Yosef's more recent Central Timna Valley Project.

entries.label: The gold of honour
entries.hint: The crown bound its officials with visible reward. At a palace 'Window of Appearances' the king personally draped a loyal servant with heavy gold collars, armlets and flies of valour before a crowd, a scene officials proudly recorded in their tombs. Service also brought land grants, a tax-exempt estate, and a permanent share ('reversion') of the offerings from a temple. The system tied the whole administrative class's prosperity directly to royal favour.
entries.note: Window of Appearances and the 'gold of honour': e.g. the Amarna tombs of Ay, Meryre and Parennefer; Ramesside examples at Thebes. Study: Alexander Binder, The Gold of Honour in New Kingdom Egypt (2008).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The chariot workshop, bronze and the first iron, glassmaking, and the tomb-cutters' craft

entries.label: The chariot workshop
entries.hint: The light chariot — a bentwood frame, a floor of interwoven leather thongs, two four- or six-spoked wheels, drawn by two horses — was the New Kingdom's decisive weapon system and a demanding piece of engineering. Six survive from Tutankhamun's tomb. It needed dedicated workshops for the woodbending, leatherwork and glue, trained wheelwrights, and a supply chain for horses, and a bronze-foundry and chariot-fitting quarter has been excavated at Pi-Ramesses.
entries.note: Tutankhamun's chariots: M.A. Littauer & J.H. Crouwel, Chariots and Related Equipment from the Tomb of Tutankhamun (1985). Pi-Ramesses metal and chariot workshops: Edgar Pusch, 'Towards a Map of Piramesse', Egyptian Archaeology 14 (1999). The 'Craft of the Charioteer', P. Anastasi I.

entries.label: Bronze at its height, iron as a curiosity
entries.hint: New Kingdom smiths worked tin bronze fluently — cast tools and weapons, hammered vessels, large statuary by the lost-wax method, and gilded 'black bronze' inlaid ware. Smelted iron, by contrast, stayed rare and precious: an iron dagger in Tutankhamun's wrappings was made from meteoric metal, and the Hittite and Mitannian kings sent small iron gifts as luxuries. Egypt would not shift to iron tools in quantity for centuries after this folio.
entries.note: Tutankhamun's iron dagger, meteoric-iron confirmed: Comelli et al., 'The meteoritic origin of Tutankhamun's iron dagger blade', Meteoritics & Planetary Science 51 (2016). Iron in the Amarna letters (EA 22, Tušratta's inventory). Bronze technology: Nicholson & Shaw (eds.), Ancient Egyptian Materials and Technology (2000) pp.149–76.

entries.label: The invention of a glass industry
entries.hint: Around the start of the New Kingdom, Egypt — together with Mitanni and the Levant — turned glass from an accidental by-product into a manufactured luxury material. Craftsmen made coloured glass from scratch in furnaces, drew it into canes, and formed small vessels around a removable clay core, imitating semi-precious stone. Excavated furnace sites at Amarna, Malkata and Pi-Ramesses show the industry organised on a near-factory basis, and glass ingots travelled the trade routes as raw stock.
entries.note: Amarna glass and faience works: Paul Nicholson, Brilliant Things for Akhenaten: The Production of Glass, Vitreous Materials and Pottery at Amarna Site O45.1 (2007). Egyptian primary glassmaking: Rehren & Pusch, 'Late Bronze Age glass production at Qantir-Piramesses', Science 308 (2005).

entries.label: Cutting and painting the royal tombs
entries.hint: The Deir el-Medina gang drove long corridor-tombs into the limestone with copper and bronze chisels, wooden mallets and dolerite pounders, hauling out the chip in baskets and lighting the work with wicks that had salt added to cut the soot. Plasterers skimmed the rough walls, draughtsmen laid out scenes on a red grid, and painters filled them in to a fixed palette. Ostraca record tools issued and returned by weight, days lost to illness, and the progress of each tomb corridor by corridor.
entries.note: Reeves & Wilkinson, The Complete Valley of the Kings (1996) pp.20–33 on technique. Tool dossiers and work journals: Černý, A Community of Workmen at Thebes (1973). Lamp experiments: Lucas & Harris, Ancient Egyptian Materials and Industries (4th ed. 1962).

entries.label: Quarrying and moving the monoliths
entries.hint: Obelisks were cut as single shafts from the Aswan granite by pounding trenches with dolerite balls; the Unfinished Obelisk, abandoned when it cracked, would have weighed over 1,000 tonnes. Finished shafts and colossi were levered onto sledges, dragged to the river, and floated downstream on purpose-built barges — Hatshepsut's Deir el-Bahari relief shows a 60-metre barge carrying two obelisks end to end, towed by twenty-seven boats. Raising them upright at the temple was done with earthen ramps and sand-filled funnels.
entries.note: Unfinished Obelisk: Engelbach, The Problem of the Obelisks (1923). Hatshepsut's obelisk-barge relief, Deir el-Bahari: Naville, The Temple of Deir el Bahari, vol. VI (1908). Amenhotep son of Hapu on moving colossi: his statue inscriptions, Urkunden IV 1820–22.

entries.label: The shaduf and the walled garden
entries.hint: New Kingdom tomb scenes give the first clear pictures of the shaduf — a bucket on a counterpoised pivoting pole — used to lift water from the river or a canal into garden plots and basin margins above the natural flood line. It let Egyptians keep irrigated ground productive through the low-water months and made the enclosed pleasure-and-produce garden, with its rectangular pool, vines, date and sycomore-fig, and imported pomegranate and olive, a standard feature of elite estates.
entries.note: Shaduf in the tomb of Ipuy (TT217) and others: Davies, Two Ramesside Tombs at Thebes (1927). Gardens: Alix Wilkinson, The Garden in Ancient Egypt (1998). New crops: Renate Germer, Flora des pharaonischen Ägypten (1985).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Amarna letters and the club of great kings, the Keftiu of the Aegean, and Punt revisited

entries.label: The Amarna letters and the great kings
entries.hint: An archive of about 380 clay tablets from Akhetaten, written in Akkadian cuneiform, preserves Egypt's foreign correspondence: letters to and from the 'great kings' of Babylonia, Assyria, Mitanni, Hatti and Alašiya, who address the pharaoh as 'brother' and haggle over gold, gifts and marriages, and letters from the small kings of Canaan pleading for troops against their neighbours and the roving Habiru. It is the fullest surviving picture of Late Bronze Age international relations.
entries.note: William L. Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992). Discovered by locals at Amarna in 1887; tablets now mainly in Berlin, London and Cairo. Cohen & Westbrook (eds.), Amarna Diplomacy (2000).

entries.label: Marrying into Egypt
entries.hint: Foreign kings sealed alliances by sending daughters to the pharaoh's harem with enormous dowries — Amenhotep III took princesses of Mitanni (Gilukhepa, then Tadukhepa), Babylon and Arzawa; Ramesses II married a daughter of the Hittite king Hattusili III with a wedding stela set up at several temples. Egypt, uniquely, refused to reciprocate: 'from of old, a daughter of the king of Egypt has not been given to anyone', the pharaoh tells Babylon — a studied diplomatic asymmetry.
entries.note: Amarna letters EA 1–5 (Babylon), EA 17–29 (Mitanni). Ramesses II's 'Marriage Stela': Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II 233–56. Analysis: Samuel Meier, 'Diplomacy and International Marriages', in Cohen & Westbrook (eds.), Amarna Diplomacy (2000).

entries.label: Keftiu — Egypt and the Aegean world
entries.hint: Eighteenth-Dynasty tomb paintings show 'Keftiu' — men in Aegean kilts carrying Cretan and Mycenaean-style vessels — among the tribute-bearers, and a statue-base from Amenhotep III's mortuary temple lists Aegean place-names including Knossos, Mycenae and Phaistos. At Tell el-Dab'a, fragments of wall paintings in pure Minoan technique and iconography, including bull-leaping, decorated an early Eighteenth-Dynasty palace — direct evidence of Aegean artists working in Egypt.
entries.note: Keftiu in the tombs of Rekhmire, Menkheperreseneb, Useramun: Wachsmann, Aegeans in the Theban Tombs (1987). Kom el-Hetan list: Elizabeth Cline, 'Amenhotep III and the Aegean', various. Tell el-Dab'a frescoes: Manfred Bietak, Nannó Marinatos & Clairy Palivou, Taureador Scenes in Tell el-Dab'a and Knossos (2007).

entries.label: Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt
entries.hint: A relief cycle on the middle terrace of Hatshepsut's temple records a state trading voyage to Punt: five ships rowed down the Red Sea, the reed-hut village on stilts and its cattle, the corpulent Puntite queen Ati, and the return cargo — myrrh, ebony, gold, panther skins, baboons, and thirty-one living incense trees with their root-balls in baskets, replanted in front of the temple. It became the model image of Egyptian long-distance trade.
entries.note: Punt reliefs: Naville, The Temple of Deir el Bahari, vol. III (1898); translation in Redford, various. On Punt's location (Sudanese/Eritrean coast or interior): Kathryn Bard & Rodolfo Fattovich, and the Mersa Gawasis evidence; Kenneth Kitchen, 'The Land of Punt', in Shaw et al. (eds.), The Archaeology of Africa (1993).

entries.label: The Uluburun ship
entries.hint: A merchant ship that sank off southern Anatolia around 1320 BC carried the material of Late Bronze exchange as a single cargo: ten tonnes of Cypriot copper in ox-hide ingots, a tonne of tin, about 175 glass ingots, Canaanite jars of terebinth resin, ebony, elephant and hippo ivory, ostrich eggshell, Baltic amber, and — among the personal items — a gold scarab inscribed for Nefertiti. It shows the interconnected trade world Egypt's gold and grain fed into.
entries.note: Excavated by the Institute of Nautical Archaeology (George Bass, Cemal Pulak), 1984–94. Pulak, 'The Uluburun shipwreck: an overview', International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 27 (1998); Yalçın, Pulak & Slotta (eds.), Das Schiff von Uluburun (2005).

entries.label: Foreign gods and words in Egypt
entries.hint: Three centuries of empire and immigration reshaped Egyptian culture from inside. Levantine deities were worshipped in Egypt in their own right — Baal and Seth merged, Reshef as a war-god, Astarte, Anat and Qadesh with temples especially in the eastern Delta. Late Egyptian filled with Canaanite loanwords for chariots, weapons, plants and abstractions. Syrians, Nubians and 'Sea People' Sherden held posts in the administration and army, and tens of thousands of war captives were settled on temple land.
entries.note: Foreign cults: Rainer Stadelmann, Syrisch-palästinensische Gottheiten in Ägypten (1967); Christiane Zivie-Coche and the Delta evidence. Loanwords: James Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts of the New Kingdom and Third Intermediate Period (1994).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Nile and the desert gold roads, the empire from Napata to the Euphrates, and the Bronze Age club of powers

entries.label: The Nile and the gold roads
entries.hint: The empire's wealth still began with the flood, but its gold came from the deserts, and kings invested in the routes: Seti I cut a rock temple and dug a well on the Barramiya road to the Eastern Desert mines, boasting in the Kanais inscription that earlier expeditions had died of thirst on that track. Well-digging, guard posts and route-marking along the Wadi Hammamat and Wadi Allaqi turned the mining hinterland into managed state landscape.
entries.note: Kanais temple and well inscription of Seti I: Schott, Kanais: Der Tempel Sethos I. im Wâdi Mia (1961); translation, Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions Translated I. Desert route infrastructure: Steven Sidebotham et al., The Red Land: The Illustrated Archaeology of Egypt's Eastern Desert (2008).

entries.label: From Napata to the Euphrates
entries.hint: At its greatest extent under Thutmose III, Egyptian power ran from the Fourth Cataract of the Nile, at Napata, to the bend of the Euphrates in northern Syria — the largest area any Egyptian state ever controlled. The temple walls at Karnak carry topographical lists naming several hundred conquered or claimed towns in Nubia and the Levant, arranged as bound captives, an administrative map of the known world as tribute-payers.
entries.note: Topographical lists: Jean Simons, Handbook for the Study of Egyptian Topographical Lists Relating to Western Asia (1937); Kenneth Kitchen and Donald Redford on the Thutmoside lists. Extent: Redford, Egypt, Canaan, and Israel in Ancient Times (1992) pp.156–91.

entries.label: The club of great powers
entries.hint: For roughly two centuries the Near East ran as a system of a few comparable kingdoms — Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni (then Assyria), Babylon, and Alašiya on Cyprus — whose kings called one another 'brother', exchanged gifts, envoys and brides, guaranteed each other's merchants, and largely respected borders. A shared palace culture, the Akkadian diplomatic language and dense trade tied them together. That very interdependence is why the system, when it failed around 1200, failed everywhere at once.
entries.note: Mario Liverani, Prestige and Interest: International Relations in the Near East ca. 1600–1100 B.C. (1990); Raymond Cohen & Raymond Westbrook (eds.), Amarna Diplomacy (2000); Eric Cline, 1177 B.C. (2014).

entries.label: The Sea Peoples appear
entries.hint: Groups the Egyptians named Sherden, Lukka, Ekwesh, Shekelesh and Teresh begin turning up in the record: Sherden raiding the Delta coast under Ramesses II, who then recruits captured Sherden into his own guard; Lukka among the Hittites' foes at Kadesh; and a coalition of them fighting alongside the Libyans against Merneptah. Behind these names lie disturbances across the Aegean and western Anatolia — the leading edge of the movements that would break on Egypt a generation later.
entries.note: Sherden under Ramesses II: the Tanis and Aswan stelae; Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II. Merneptah's coalition: the Great Karnak Inscription. Overview: Nancy Sandars, The Sea Peoples (1985); Cline, 1177 B.C. (2014).

entries.label: The drying of the eastern Mediterranean
entries.hint: Pollen cores from the Levant and Anatolia and other proxies point to a run of drier, cooler decades across the eastern Mediterranean from the mid-13th century — years in which the Hittite king wrote to Ugarit and Egypt for emergency grain, 'it is a matter of life or death'. Egypt, watered by a river fed from tropical Africa rather than local rain, was better buffered than its neighbours, but the same stress fed the migrations and food crises pressing on its frontiers.
entries.note: Kaniewski et al., 'Environmental roots of the Late Bronze Age crisis', PLoS ONE 8 (2013); Drake, 'The influence of climatic change on the Late Bronze Age Collapse', Journal of Archaeological Science 39 (2012). Hittite grain requests: RS 20.212 and related Ugarit texts.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Hatshepsut and Nefertiti, the tomb-workers of Deir el-Medina, and the foreign women of the harem

entries.label: Hatshepsut before and beneath the crown
entries.hint: Before she was king, Hatshepsut was a king's daughter, a king's chief wife, and God's Wife of Amun, a powerful priestly office with its own estates. As ruler she legitimated a woman on the throne partly through her steward and confidant Senenmut, who held dozens of titles and tutored her daughter Neferure, and partly through reliefs at Deir el-Bahari claiming Amun as her physical father. Her nephew-stepson Thutmose III served under her for two decades before ruling alone.
entries.note: Senenmut: Peter Dorman, The Monuments of Senenmut (1988) and The Tombs of Senenmut (1991). Divine-birth reliefs: Naville, Deir el Bahari II (1896). Catherine Roehrig (ed.), Hatshepsut: From Queen to Pharaoh (2005).

entries.label: Nefertiti and the family as icon
entries.hint: Nefertiti appears in Amarna art at a scale and in roles normally reserved for the king — offering to the Aten, riding a chariot, even smiting a captive — and the tender scenes of Akhenaten, Nefertiti and their six daughters under the sun's rays were themselves a form of religious statement. She drops out of the visible record a few years before Akhenaten's death; whether she died, fell from favour, or became the co-king Neferneferuaten is unresolved.
entries.note: Dorothea Arnold, The Royal Women of Amarna (1996); Joyce Tyldesley, Nefertiti: Egypt's Sun Queen (1998). The smiting scene: a talatat block from Hermopolis. Bust: Berlin ÄM 21300.

entries.label: Queen Tiye
entries.hint: Tiye, chief wife of Amenhotep III, came from a non-royal family — her parents Yuya and Thuya were buried in the Valley of the Kings in a tomb found nearly intact in 1905. She was unusually visible in her husband's reign, shown at his scale and named on his commemorative scarabs, and she remained a political presence into her son Akhenaten's reign, when the Mitannian king Tushratta wrote to her directly, urging her to keep relations warm.
entries.note: Tomb of Yuya and Thuya (KV46): Quibell, The Tomb of Yuaa and Thuiu (1908). Tiye in the Amarna letters: EA 26 (Tushratta to Tiye). Kozloff & Bryan (eds.), Egypt's Dazzling Sun (1992).

entries.label: The people of Deir el-Medina
entries.hint: The village archive lets individual workmen be followed across decades: the literate scribe Ramose and his adopted heir Qenherkhepeshef, the foreman Neferhotep, the 'servant in the Place of Truth' Sennedjem whose small tomb has some of the best-preserved painting from Egypt. Their letters and notes record wives managing the grain and the household while the men were away at the tomb for eight-day shifts, loans between neighbours, feuds, adultery cases, and a persistent shortage of donkeys.
entries.note: Sennedjem's tomb (TT1): Bruyère, Tombe no. 1 de Sen-nedjem (1959). Community studies: Lynn Meskell, Private Life in New Kingdom Egypt (2002); A.G. McDowell, Village Life in Ancient Egypt (1999).

entries.label: The women of the harem and the weaving houses
entries.hint: The royal harem was a productive institution as much as a domestic one. Foreign princesses arrived with hundreds of attendants; captured Levantine and Nubian women were assigned to it as weavers and concubines. The harem-palace at Mi-wer, modern Gurob, in the Faiyum, ran large linen workshops and estates and raised royal children. A Ramesside deed, the Adoption Papyrus, shows a childless woman first adopting her husband's children by a slave, then freeing and adopting the slave's family — a rare close view of unfree domestic life.
entries.note: Gurob: Petrie, Kahun, Gurob and Hawara (1890) and Illahun, Kahun and Gurob (1891); Gurob Harem Palace Project (Ian Shaw). Adoption Papyrus (P. Ashmolean 1945.96): Gardiner, 'Adoption Extraordinary', JEA 26 (1940).

entries.label: Amenhotep son of Hapu, the commoner made a god
entries.hint: Amenhotep, son of Hapu, a scribe from a modest Delta family, rose under Amenhotep III to be overseer of all the king's works — directing the quarrying and hauling of the Colossi of Memnon among much else — and was rewarded with the rare honour of his own mortuary temple among the kings' on the Theban west bank. A thousand years later he was still being worshipped, alongside the Old Kingdom architect Imhotep, as a god of healing and wisdom.
entries.note: Statues of Amenhotep son of Hapu (Cairo): Urkunden IV 1813–35. His mortuary temple: Robichon & Varille, Le temple du scribe royal Amenhotep fils de Hapou (1936). Later cult: Wildung, Egyptian Saints: Deification in Pharaonic Egypt (1977).
